introductoryArticles.title: AN IDEA. A SCREEN. A START.
introductoryArticles.description: Every site you use began as someone’s idea. Learn what goes into building one — then try a small move of your own.

steps.title: Three parts of a page
steps.body: HTML gives a page structure. CSS gives it its look. JavaScript adds interactions. You don’t have to learn all three at once.

steps.title: Try one tiny build
steps.body: Sketch a page for an interest you care about. Give it a clear heading, a short introduction and one useful action. Think about someone using it on a small phone.

steps.title: Build for other people
steps.body: Readable text, keyboard access, clear labels and good contrast are part of building well. Start with a free learning resource and never pay for a course without checking it with a trusted person.

introductoryArticles.takeaway: Start small. Make one useful thing. Improve it.

introductoryArticles.title: MAKE SOMETHING MOVE.
introductoryArticles.description: Code meets the physical world. Robots are built from small systems — and curious people.

steps.title: Sense. Decide. Act.
steps.body: A sensor reads something, code makes a decision and an output responds. A light that reacts to brightness is already a useful first project.

steps.title: A safe first step
steps.body: Try a browser-based electronics simulator or a supervised beginner workshop. Leave mains power, batteries, moving machinery and specialist tools to appropriately trained supervision.

steps.title: More than one role
steps.body: Robotics can involve software, mechanical design, electronics, testing and teamwork. You can start with the part that interests you.

introductoryArticles.takeaway: Curiosity counts more than already knowing the answer.

introductoryArticles.title: YOUR IDEAS. NEW TOOLS.
introductoryArticles.description: Design, editing, animation and sound all have a place in tech. You don’t need to pick between creative and technical.

steps.title: Tell one clear story
steps.body: Plan a 20-second sequence using drawings or objects. A beginning, a change and an ending are enough to practise storytelling.

steps.title: Respect people and rights
steps.body: Ask before recording someone. Don’t include anyone’s private information. Use your own work or material you have permission to use.

steps.title: Keep a small portfolio
steps.body: A few thoughtful projects can show what you enjoy and how you improve. Keep personal contact details private and ask a trusted adult before publishing work that identifies you.

introductoryArticles.takeaway: Make it yours. Make it with care.

introductoryArticles.title: MORE THAN THE SCORE.
introductoryArticles.description: Sport can be about enjoyment, routine and belonging. You don’t need to be the best person in the room to belong there.

steps.title: Find a good environment
steps.body: Look for verified supervision, age-appropriate sessions and a coach who treats everyone with respect. Ask about accessibility, costs and equipment.

steps.title: Choose your own progress
steps.body: A goal could be showing up regularly, learning a skill or enjoying movement. Compare your progress with your own starting point.

steps.title: Look after yourself
steps.body: Use suitable equipment and follow a qualified coach’s guidance. Stop and tell the responsible adult if something hurts or feels unsafe.

introductoryArticles.takeaway: Your pace. Your progress. Your place on the team.

introductoryArticles.title: THE GAME HAS MORE ROLES.
introductoryArticles.description: Not every route in sport is professional playing. Coaching, officiating, events and creative work all help a game happen.

steps.title: Look around the pitch
steps.body: Think about who organises a session, cares for the venue, runs the scoreboard or tells the story afterwards. Different strengths fit different roles.

steps.title: Learn under supervision
steps.body: Age limits, qualifications and safeguarding requirements vary. Find an official governing body or verified provider and ask about appropriate introductory routes.

steps.title: Ask practical questions
steps.body: What does training cost? Is it recognised? Who supervises? What support is available? Don’t accept promises of guaranteed trials, contracts or jobs.

introductoryArticles.takeaway: You can be part of the game in more than one way.

introductoryArticles.title: FIND YOUR RHYTHM.
introductoryArticles.description: A short walk, a coached sprint session or non-contact fitness. Movement can fit around who you are.

steps.title: Start where you are
steps.body: Try an activity that suits your access needs and experience. A qualified provider should be able to explain adaptations and suitable starting points.

steps.title: A routine that works for you
steps.body: Small, realistic plans are easier to return to. Rest, food, sleep and support matter too.

steps.title: Know when to get advice
steps.body: If you have a health concern, ask a qualified health professional about what is appropriate for you. A sports session is not a substitute for medical or mental-health care.

introductoryArticles.takeaway: Movement is an option, not a test of your worth.

introductoryArticles.title: SKILLS YOU CAN BUILD ON.
introductoryArticles.description: From carpentry to construction design, practical work brings ideas into the world. Start with safe, supervised learning.

steps.title: Get a feel for the work
steps.body: A verified taster session can help you explore measuring, planning, materials and design before committing to a course.

steps.title: Safety is part of the skill
steps.body: Tools and workshops require training, suitable supervision and protective equipment. Don’t practise hazardous tasks alone or use equipment without permission.

steps.title: Check the next step
steps.body: Ask a school careers adviser, college or official training provider about recognised routes, entry requirements, support and costs.

introductoryArticles.takeaway: A practical skill is a place to start, not a limit on your future.

introductoryArticles.title: LEARN. WORK. KEEP GROWING.
introductoryArticles.description: An apprenticeship combines work and training. It is worth understanding the details before making a decision.

steps.title: What to look for
steps.body: Check the employer, recognised qualification, training provider, entry requirements and working arrangements. Eligibility varies; use the official government apprenticeship service.

steps.title: Ask about the whole offer
steps.body: Hours, pay, travel, support, study time and accessibility all matter. A trusted careers adviser can help you compare options without pressure.

steps.title: No guaranteed places here
steps.body: RWM’s demo listings do not offer real apprenticeships. Visit GOV.UK’s apprenticeship pages or your school or college careers team for current opportunities.

introductoryArticles.takeaway: A good opportunity should stand up to clear questions.

introductoryArticles.title: TURN AN INTEREST INTO A SKILL.
introductoryArticles.description: Design, video, music and youth enterprise all begin with something you can practise. Learn the work behind the finished thing.

steps.title: Work to a small brief
steps.body: Design a poster for an imaginary event. Who is it for, what do they need to know and what should they do next? Keep it readable on a phone.

steps.title: Understand agreements
steps.body: Before real paid work, ask a trusted adviser about payment, permissions, contracts and age-specific requirements. Don’t share financial or identity documents with someone you haven’t checked.

steps.title: Explore without pressure
steps.body: A supervised course, careers conversation or volunteering role may help you learn. Ask about expenses and expectations. Your time has value.

introductoryArticles.takeaway: An interest is a start. Practice gives it shape.
